title: Accurate Atomic Correlation Energies and Virial Trends for Correlation-Consistent Effective Core Potentials III: Quantitative Separation of Fixed-Node Biases and Localization Errors in Cs-Rn
abstract: Atomic benchmarks for sixth-period elements (Cs-Rn) are established to sub-millihartree precision under correlation-consistent effective core potentials (ccECPs) using coupled-cluster [up to CCSDT(Q)] and full configuration interaction methods. These references systematically characterize electron correlation, potential-to-kinetic energy partitioning, and combined fixed-node and locality biases ($η$) in fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo (FNDMC). The valence kinetic-to-total energy ratio ($ξ$) departs from the non-relativistic all-electron Coulombic virial limit ($ξ=100\%$), remaining confined between 25.8$\%$ and 37.6$\%$. The Un-pseudizing of semi-core shells decreases $ξ$ as the attractive potential energy deepens faster than the accompanying kinetic energy escalates. Periodic trends in $ξ$ reveal a $5d$ plateau near 34$\%$, with a lanthanide-contraction-driven maximum in Hf, followed by a sharp decline across the $6p$ block. In FNDMC, $η$ escalates rapidly at the onset of group-1/2 and toward the $6p$ closed-shell limit, peaking at 5.42$\%$ in Rn. Although fixed-node errors dominate $η$ in most sixth-period elements, a locality error inversion occurs in Bi, with Pb exhibiting comparable error magnitudes. Furthermore, core-valence partitioning alters trial wavefunction nodal topology: in Tl, three-dimensional nodal cross-sections reveal isolated toroidal domains that confine walkers. This work completes the periodic-table-wide ccECP database from H to Rn, revealing how pseudopotential choices govern energy partitioning, nodal topology, and the balance between fixed-node and localization errors.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive, high-precision database for the electronic structure of heavy sixth-period elements (Cs-Rn) using effective core potentials. It rigorously quantifies how electron correlation energy is partitioned between kinetic and potential terms, and critically separates the inherent fixed-node error from the localization error in Quantum Monte Carlo simulations. This provides crucial insight into the limitations of current many-body approximations for heavy atoms.
main_problem: The paper aims to systematically characterize electron correlation, potential-to-kinetic energy partitioning, and combined fixed-node and locality biases in Quantum Monte Carlo calculations for heavy elements.
main_result: It establishes a periodic-table-wide database for sixth-period elements (Cs-Rn), quantifying how pseudopotential choices govern energy partitioning and the balance between fixed-node and localization errors.
method: The study combines high-level correlated many-body methods (CCSDT(Q), FCI) for benchmarks with Fixed-Node Diffusion Monte Carlo (FNDMC) to analyze systematic errors.
model_or_system: The system under study is the electronic structure of sixth-period elements (Cs-Rn) modeled using correlation-consistent effective core potentials (ccECPs).
key_observables: Kinetic-to-Total Energy Ratio ($\xi$), combined fixed-node and locality biases ($\eta$), and the separation of fixed-node ($\epsilon_{	ext{FN}}$) and localization ($\epsilon_{	ext{loc}}$) errors.
important_parameters: The analysis spans the entire sixth period, revealing trends like a $5d$ plateau and a sharp decline across the $6p$ block.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the single-reference Slater-Jastrow trial wavefunction and the fixed-node approximation in FNDMC.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ratio $\xi$ vs. core size, and 3D cross-sections of nodal hypersurfaces, showing increasing topological complexity with $Z_{	ext{eff}}$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes high-precision benchmarks for Cs-Rn, then systematically analyzes the energy partitioning ($\xi$) and error sources ($\eta$) in FNDMC, culminating in a comprehensive, periodic-table-wide database.
why_interesting: While focused on heavy atoms, the rigorous error decomposition techniques ($\epsilon_{	ext{FN}}$ vs. $\epsilon_{	ext{loc}}$) are foundational to accurately modeling strongly correlated systems where electron-electron interactions are paramount.
